blog.title: Why Most SEO Campaigns Fail in the First 6 Months
blog.excerpt: It is rarely the budget. It is the order of operations. Here are the mistakes that stall SEO before it has a chance to work.
blog.body:
Most SEO campaigns do not fail because SEO stopped working. They fail because the work is done in the wrong order, measured with the wrong numbers or abandoned right before it starts paying off.

1. Content before foundation

Publishing articles on a site that Google struggles to crawl is like stocking shelves in a store with a locked front door. If key pages are blocked, slow, duplicated or buried six clicks deep, new content will not perform. Fix crawlability, indexation and internal linking first.

2. Targeting keywords without intent

A keyword with high volume is useless if the people searching it do not want what you sell. Every target should be checked against the current results page: if Google shows guides and you have a sales page, you are fighting the algorithm instead of working with it.

3. One page trying to rank for everything

Service pages that list ten services rarely rank for any of them. Each meaningful service, location and audience deserves its own page with a clear job. This is also how you avoid keyword cannibalization, where several of your own pages compete for the same search.

4. Measuring the wrong thing

Rankings and traffic are leading indicators, not outcomes. Track calls, form submissions, booked appointments and revenue from organic search. When the report connects to money, decisions get easier.

5. Quitting at month four

SEO compounds. Months one to three are mostly fixes and foundations, months four to six bring the first meaningful movement and the real returns usually show after that. Most campaigns that fail are stopped just before the curve bends.

The fix

Audit first, prioritize by impact, build pages with one clear job, earn real authority and measure revenue. It is not glamorous, but it is how rankings become an asset instead of an expense.

blog.title: The Local SEO Checklist for Service Businesses
blog.excerpt: A practical checklist to win the Google map pack: profile, citations, reviews, pages and links, in the order that matters.
blog.body:
The map pack is where local customers decide who to call. This checklist covers the work that moves map rankings, in the order we do it for clients.

Google Business Profile

  • Choose the most specific primary category that matches your main service.
  • Add every service you offer with a short description.
  • Upload real photos of your team, vehicles, location and work every month.
  • Post at least weekly: offers, projects, tips and updates.
  • Answer common questions in the Q&A section before customers ask.

Consistency across the web

Your business name, address and phone number should match exactly across your website, Google, Apple Maps, Bing, Yelp, Facebook and industry directories. Inconsistent listings confuse both customers and search engines.

Reviews

  • Ask every happy customer, with a direct link, at the moment of satisfaction.
  • Respond to every review within a few days, positive or negative.
  • Never buy reviews or offer incentives that break platform rules.

Location and service pages

Create a page for each core service and each important area you serve. Include real details: projects completed nearby, local regulations, travel times and photos. Avoid copying the same page and swapping city names.

Local links

Sponsor local teams and events, join your chamber of commerce, partner with complementary businesses and pitch local news stories. Local links are a strong prominence signal that most competitors ignore.

Track the right way

Map rankings change by location. Use a grid-based rank tracker to see visibility across your whole service area, not just at your office.

blog.title: Technical SEO Basics Every Business Owner Should Know
blog.excerpt: You do not need to be a developer to understand what holds a website back. Five technical basics, explained in plain English.
blog.body:
Technical SEO sounds intimidating, but the core ideas are simple: Google needs to find your pages, understand them and load them quickly. Here is what to check.

1. Can Google find your pages?

Every important page should be linked from somewhere on your site and listed in your XML sitemap. Pages nobody links to, called orphan pages, are hard for Google to discover. Use our Sitemap Checker to review your sitemap.

2. Are you blocking anything by accident?

Your robots.txt file tells crawlers what they may visit. One wrong line can block an entire section. Test important URLs with our Robots.txt Checker.

3. Is each page unique?

Duplicate pages split ranking signals. Use canonical tags to point duplicates to the main version and give each page a unique title and description. Our Meta Tag Checker shows these quickly.

4. Is the site fast on phones?

Google evaluates the mobile version of your site first. Large images, heavy scripts and slow hosting hurt both rankings and conversions. Compress images, use modern formats and remove scripts you do not need.

5. Does Google understand what you are?

Structured data, or schema markup, labels your business, services, products, reviews and FAQs in a format search engines read directly. It can unlock rich results. Validate yours with our Schema Checker.

When to get help

If pages will not index, traffic dropped after a redesign or your site is slow despite fixes, it is time for a professional technical SEO review.
